title: Lesson 1. 을 / 를 — the thing you act on

blocks.md:
When a verb acts **on** something, that something gets tagged with **을** or **를**.

커피**를** 마셔요.  — I drink coffee.
밥**을** 먹어요.  — I eat rice.
**을** after a consonant  ·  **를** after a vowel

**Only verbs that act on something take 을/를.** 가다, 있다, 자다 do not act on anything — nothing gets the tag. 학교를 가요 is something you will hear, but 학교**에** 가요 is the form to learn: going has a destination, not an object.

items.tip: I read a book every day.
I meet a friend. In Korean the friend is acted on — so 를, not 에게.

blocks.q: “I eat rice.”  밥 ends in ㅂ, a consonant.
blocks.why: A consonant takes **을**. 밥를 uses the vowel form; 밥이 marks it as the subject, which would mean the rice is doing the eating; 밥에 would mark a place or time.
커피 ends in a vowel → **를**. **을** is the same tag after a consonant, **가** marks a subject, **에** marks place or time.

blocks.q: Match each noun with the object tag it takes.
Build “I watch a movie.”

blocks.meaning: I watch a movie on the weekend.
blocks.why: 영화 ends in a vowel → **를**. **을** is the consonant form, **가** marks a subject, **에서** marks a place where something happens.

blocks.q: Which sentence does **not** need 을/를?
blocks.why: 가다 does not act on anything — school is a destination, so it takes **에**. The other three all have something being eaten, read or watched.

blocks.q: Write it yourself: **“I read a book every day.”**  (every day = 매일)
blocks.hint: The book is the thing being read — so it takes the object tag. 책 ends in a consonant.
blocks.why: 저는 매일 책을 읽어요. Dropping 저는 is perfectly natural in Korean when it is obvious who you mean.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “I read a book every day.”

title: Lesson 2. 은 / 는 — what you are talking about

blocks.md:
You have been using this since your first sentence:

**저는** 학생이에요.

**은/는** puts a noun up front and says: *this is what I am talking about.* English often reaches for “as for…”.

저**는** 커피를 마셔요.  — **As for me**, I drink coffee.

**은** after a consonant  ·  **는** after a vowel

선생님**은**  ·  저**는**

**Do not worry yet about 은/는 versus 이/가.** That comparison is real, and it has a whole course of its own later. Right now one habit carries you a long way: **use 은/는 on the person or thing your sentence is about, usually at the very front.**

items.tip: As for me, I am Korean.
My younger sibling is a student.
Today, I have no time. 은/는 can mark time too — “as for today”.

blocks.md:
Put 은/는 on two things and the sentence sets them against each other.

커피**는** 좋아해요. 그런데 차**는** 안 좋아해요.
— I like coffee. But tea, I don’t.

blocks.q: “My friend is a doctor.”  친구 ends in ㅜ, a vowel.
blocks.why: A vowel takes **는**. 친구은 uses the consonant form; **를** marks something acted on, and 이에요 does not act on anything; **에** marks place or time.
오늘 ends in a consonant → **은**, setting today apart from other days. **는** is the vowel form, **을** marks an object, **에** marks time — but 오늘 is one of the words that refuses 에.

blocks.q: Build “As for me, I drink coffee.”

blocks.meaning: My younger sibling is a student.
blocks.why: 동생 ends in ㅇ, a consonant → **은**. **는** is the vowel form, **이** marks a subject, **을** marks an object.

blocks.q: “커피는 좋아해요. 그런데 차는 안 좋아해요.” What is 은/는 doing here?
options: setting two things against each other
blocks.why: Two 는 in a row sets up a contrast — coffee yes, tea no. Acting on something is 을/를, a place is 에/에서, a time is 에.

blocks.q: Write it yourself: **“As for me, I like coffee.”**  (like = 좋아해요)
blocks.hint: You are the one the sentence is about, and the coffee is what you act on.
blocks.why: 저는 커피를 좋아해요. Swap 커피를 for 커피는 and you add a contrast — “coffee I like (but something else, not so much).”

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “As for me, I like coffee.”

title.en: Lesson 3. Putting Both Particles in One Sentence

blocks.md:
In Korean, the natural sentence order is **Subject/Topic → Object → Verb** (SOV).

Now you can combine **은/는** and **을/를** together to build complete sentences:

**[ Topic + 은/는 ] + [ Object + 을/를 ] + [ Verb ]**

Remember the vowel/consonant rule:
- **Topic:** 받침 있음 → **은**, 받침 없음 → **는**
- **Object:** 받침 있음 → **을**, 받침 없음 → **를**

items.tip: I learn Korean. (저 + 는, 한국어 + 를)
My friend buys bread. (친구 + 는, 빵 + 을)
Yujin reads the newspaper. (유진 + 은, 신문 + 을)

blocks.q: Which sentence has both particles attached correctly? (지민 = consonant ending, 영화 = vowel ending)
blocks.why: 지민 ends in consonant ㄴ → **은**. 영화 ends in vowel ㅘ → **를**.

blocks.q: Pair each noun with its correct particle combination.

blocks.why: 동생 ends in consonant ㅇ, so it takes topic marker **은**.

blocks.q: Attach the object particle to 물 (water): 「저는 ___ 마셔요.」
blocks.why: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ (받침), so it takes the object particle **-을** → **물을**. 물를 is the wrong form, and 물에 marks place/destination.

blocks.q: Arrange the words to say: “I eat lunch.”
Read out loud clearly: “I study Korean at the library.”

title.en: Lesson 4. Never Confusing 은/는 and 을/를

blocks.h: Topic vs. Object: Who vs. What
blocks.md:
How do you avoid mixing up **은/는** and **을/를**?

- Ask: **“Who is doing the action or being discussed?”** → Use **은/는** (e.g., 저는, 친구는).
- Ask: **“What is being eaten, bought, read, or watched?”** → Use **을/를** (e.g., 밥을, 책을).

If you swap them, the sentence turns upside down!
Notice that **은/는** can replace **을/를** when making a contrast! When you say **“사과는 좋아해요”**, it means: *Apples, I like (but something else, I might not)*.

items.tip: Suji listens to music. — Suji is topic (는), music is object (를).

items.ch: 라면은 먹어요. 그런데 김밥은 안 먹어요.
items.tip: Ramen I eat. But kimbap I don’t. — 은/는 shows contrast on foods.
The teacher buys apples. — 선생님 is topic (은), 사과 is object (를).

blocks.q: Which sentence means “My friend meets a teacher”?
blocks.why: 친구 is the one doing the action (topic: 는), and 선생님 is the person being met (object: 을).

blocks.q: In the sentence “저는 영화를 봐요”, what does 영화를 tell you?
options: It is the object being watched
It is the location of the action
It is the time of the action
blocks.why: The particle **-를** marks the direct object of the verb 봐요 (watch).

blocks.q: Match each sentence with its correct English meaning.
pairs: Pizza, I like (contrasting with other foods).

blocks.sentence: 지수는 책[을] 읽고, 민호는 음악을 들어요.
blocks.meaning: Jisu reads a book, and Minho listens to music.
blocks.why: 책 ends in a consonant and is the direct object of 읽다, so it takes **-을**.

blocks.q: You are talking about yourself drinking tea: 「저는 차___ 마셔요.」
blocks.why: 차 ends in a vowel and is the direct object acted on by 마시다, so attach **-를** → **차를**. 차을 uses the wrong vowel form, and 차에 marks place/time.

blocks.say: 저는 한국 영화는 좋아하지만 미국 영화는 잘 안 봐요.
blocks.rom: jeo-neun han-guk yeong-hwa-neun joh-a-ha-ji-man mi-guk yeong-hwa-neun jal an bwa-yo
blocks.q: Say it out loud with contrast: “As for Korean movies I like them, but as for American movies I rarely watch them.”
Arrange the words to say: “Yujin buys shoes.”
